title: Chapter One - Waking Up

blocks.text: In the infinite black nothing, was a small surge: a pinprick of light expanding…
Expanding…
Pulsing…
Reaching…
Coagulating into a mind shape.
Sensations flicking on and off in the darkness.
Distant flashes.

Forcing attention: the breath pulling into and pushing out of widened nostrils, aching neck trying to roll a heavy head on some soft comfortable surface, a copper-metallic taste and smell. A sore throat… dry lips tearing open a layer of skin binding them. A gasp of air through an arid mouth… Awareness expanding rapidly. Connecting each piece into one experience… a body. My body…
My body waking up. Now all at once. Consciousness hit. My body.

I was feeling that sludgy-thick resistance now that comes with snapping back to the conscious world after an indeterminate amount of time in the unconscious one. I tried to open my eyes but the room felt so bright and my eyelids so heavy. My head involuntarily swiveled from side to side on my aching neck, trying to find a comfortable opening to emerge into. Even after my eyelids lightened up enough to open, they snapped shut again to defend against the piercing light of the outside world. My arm, in automatic reaction, attempted to shield my eyes against the brightness, my muscles resisted enough to need noticeable effort to oblige.

A flicker of worry jumped into my mind, but my focus on the effort to move pushed it away. My whole body felt heavy and foreign, but I was finally able to lift my arm to shield my eyes. I looked out at a blurry world through slitted eyes and cracks in my fingers: my entire face trying to compress my eyelids to keep out the bright pain. Shapes refused to coagulate from their dissolved cloudy state. I rubbed my eyes and attempted again… and again.

The room was a series of blobs and smears of color: faint turquoise walls, green bunches blotted about, a brown and blue stack in a corner and a massive source of light directly in front of me. Slowly, the green smears along the ceiling resolved into twisting stems and leaves. The green bunches were other potted plants pushed against the calming blue-green walls. Sunlight spilled in through a window at the far end of the room that took up the entire wall.

The world was still focusing—rendering—when I put my hands out to examine them. When they came into focus, a small green bracelet around my left wrist caught my attention for a moment before I noticed IVs sticking out of my arms. Purple liquid pumped into my left arm and a clear liquid into my right.

My breathing got heavier and my chest started to rise and fall more violently. I looked down at the rest of my body lying in a small bed in the middle of the room, covered by a white sheet with a small blue blanket on top of that. I had to fight my body once more when I tried to sit upright. My feeble arms resisted, but I overcame them, feeling a light pinch where the IVs went into the crease of my elbow.

I was starting to experience a particularly acute type of dread that comes when your consciousness opens into a hospital bed without memory of how you got there—or, in my case, who the you was that was sitting there. I reached into my memory like groping the darkness, and came up empty-handed for anything to establish a self outside of this current moment.

It took an unusual amount of strength to lift the sheet covering me and reveal a skinny body underneath. It was wearing a light grey two-piece sweatsuit. I examined the rest of the room for any other clues as to where I was or why but didn’t see any commonplace hospital items besides my IVs. The IVs stretched away behind my bed, to some unseen end. I hurriedly flexed my extremities. My body, though obstinate, moved with some coaxing. I let out a sigh and fell back into the pillow, only basking for a moment in relief before the void in my mind, where my memories should be, pushed back into my awareness.

I lifted my shaking body upright against considerable resistance and swung my feet over the edge of the bed. The IV in my right arm tightened for a moment before slackening again. My right pant leg had gotten pulled up, revealing an atrophied and weak-looking calf. I was determined to find answers and they didn’t seem to be here. I wiggled my toes and spun my ankles to test them again. Then, I pushed through the pain and edged a bit more off the bed. The floor felt soft against the bottoms of my feet. It had the friction of rubber but the look of marble tile. I felt my core tightening as I fought toppling over in any direction.

I got my body under a loose sense of control. I prepared to lean my weight onto my feet for my first steps toward answers, until a hissing noise came from a wooden part of the wall directly in front of me sliding aside, into a pocket in the wall. Accompanying the sound, a woman came walking through the fresh opening carrying some sort of tablet-like device. She wore pastel salmon-colored scrubs and had dreads tied into a bundle on top of her head with accents of beads and metal wraps throughout. Her eyes were shining above a full lipped smile. I’m sure I looked startled.
“Hello, Christian!” She spoke softly with a pleasant lilt.
All I could muster was a confused stare at her while I cleared my throat.
“I saw on the monitors that you were awake…” She trailed off glancing down at a tablet-like device she was holding.
Her eyes lifted back toward me. “How are you feeling today?”
Her accent was faint and unfamiliar, just enough to make certain words land noticeably outside what I was used to.
“I feel…” I garbled out through my restricted throat. I tried again: “I feel—”
“No, no, no. It’s okay. Don’t try to speak. I’m sorry, I shouldn’t have asked you to talk so soon.” She chuckled at herself. “Your body needs more time to recover.”

She crossed to a sink built into the wall and pressed a small button. “I’m sure you’re disoriented too,” she said looking back over her shoulder as the pitch of gurgling water rose, “It’s going to take some time before you’re back to balance again.”
She brought the cup over while I rubbed my throat and tried to clear it with gentle grunting noises.
“Here is some water.” She radiated a disarmingly kind nature.

Until the liquid hit my lips and slid down my sandy throat, I hadn’t realized how thirsty I truly was. It was a mixture of light pain and soothing satisfaction, like scratching an itch. I drank too fast to breathe and had to stop halfway through to gulp in air. The water had a pleasantly sweet aftertaste.
As I chugged, she asked, “Do you remember me, Christian?”

My eyes were fixed on the ceiling while I poured the second half of the liquid down my aching throat. I descended into a coughing fit as I choked on the last gulp. I looked back to her with my elbow raised, partially covering my coughing mouth. I shook my head from side to side and grunted something like “no.” She understood.
She gave a compassionate nod, “My name is Angela. I am your attendant today. I know this is all probably quite disorienting, but we are here to help you through your recovery.”
After I had finished gasping for air and clearing my throat again, through labored breath, I gestured for another drink.

She only smiled and replied, “We have to let that drink settle into your stomach for now. You’ve been asleep for quite a while and I want to make sure your stomach can handle it before we fill it up.”
It took immense effort but I asked, “What… happened?” I was cut off by coughs again.
“You have some memory loss. Don’t worry, this is completely normal and it’s often temporary.”
“Often tem…temp…?” I said, my stress rising and my throat restricting even more with it.

Her tone and demeanor softened, “Your brain structure is fully functional and intact. Sometimes full cognitive function just takes time. We have you on a treatment with a high success rate for rebuilding your body and mind.”
Rebuilding my body and mind?
“What… happened?” I pushed again.
She gave a soft sigh, “It’s important now to rest. If you need us for anything, there is a button… oh.”
Her arm extended under the bed and pulled up a small sort of railing that locked into place. There were multiple buttons on it with different pictographs.
“Here they are… This one is to call on us. This one is to call for dietary… for food, and this one is if you’re having any pain.” She pointed to each button as she explained them.
“Can’t… remember.”
She caste a sympathetic look my way before she fiddled with the tablet. “Well, your name is Christian Talima. You were in a coma.”
That word hit my chest like a ton of bricks. Coma. I could feel my body flushing with blood, then getting cold and clammy.
“Focus on rest right now.” She put her hand on my shoulder.
Fear tightened my throat and stomach again. I wanted to ask “What happened” again, but my body wasn’t really able to. My throat felt tight and I almost seemed to feel a light shiver coming on.
Instead, I asked, “Walk?” It was a question for her and me.

I started putting weight on my legs and instantly pain shot through them and almost toppled me. I struggled to use my similarly atrophied arms to stabilize myself again, but the attendant deftly slid her hands under my armpits and guided me back upright. The tablet was now dangling from her wrist by a leash and bumping against my side. Each time it hit my body I felt a sharp jolt of discomfort barely under the threshold of pain.

“Your limbs have atrophied. You can’t use them normally until you’ve healed more.” She was slightly more terse than before. I apologized as I tried to use my arms to assist her in settling me back into the bed.

She continued, “You’re on a therapy that will get your body back into shape rapidly, but it means you need to rest for now.” Her hand was on my shoulder, stabilizing my now aching body but, it felt like I was being held with a subtle electric squeeze.
I only nodded dejectedly.
“Please just give it more time,” she finished.

I would have probably had a million more questions, but my throat wasn’t cooperating. My body felt so heavy and obstinate. All I could really do was sit in the bed as the fear and worry bounced off the inner boundaries of my skull.

She was looking at the tablet somewhat confusedly as her fingers pecked away slowly at whatever she was typing. Her face was making various expressions of concentration and satisfaction as she nodded.
I forced out a question, “Water?”
Her attention moved back to me very deliberately. “How does your stomach feel?”
I gave a wincing thumbs up.
She looked at me confused.
“Fine…” I clarified in a rasp.
“Well we should—”
“Well… a tingle…” I gestured toward my throat. “Here…”, then my stomach. I waved my hands gesturing to my general body.
“That’s good. It means the therapy is active. I adjusted it slightly, but your body needs time to get used to it. I think we should still wait a little longer before you ingest anything else…”
I instinctively looked down at the purple IV in my left arm. The green braided bracelet caught my attention again. It was some sort of green fabric wrapped around itself then braided.
She looked at the screen again, then back to me, “We should wait a bit longer. If you’re worried about hydration…” she pointed to the IV I had just been looking at. “The IV is providing that.”
“Food?” I forced.
She shook her head solemnly. “I can bring you a nutritional soup in around 2 hours.”

I nodded, my shoulders slumping into my new reality, giving in to her authority as caretaker. She was just tapping away at the tablet. Her typing was very odd. She was pecking away one finger at a time after searching for each letter. As she was typing she would look back up to observe me.

I wanted to ask what she was doing on the tablet but my throat restricted further communication. I could feel my breathing intensifying and tried to move my focus away from it to look around the room again. The entire room was bathed in warm golden light. The walls were a subtle turquoise color accentuated by the various plant life strewn about the room; planters were built into the windowsills and hanging from the ceiling. There was a guitar propped up on a stand next to a shallow window bay that housed booth seating and a small table. It looked like a little cafe seating area. I looked back to Angela and found her staring at me. She gave a gentle smile and I returned it. She lifted her cupped hands up as if she was scooping the air in front of her as she demonstratively breathed in deeply, then lowered her hand, as if dumping the contents onto the floor as she sighed out her breath. She repeated this a few times before I realized she was doing this to get me to follow. I obliged, forcing my breathing to slow to match hers. We did this for a while. I did feel much calmer now. I again noticed this sort of buzzing feeling in my body. This time it felt almost like a low calming humming tone. Was this part of the therapy?

She did some sort of entry into the tablet again. As she looked down at the tablet she spoke to me “If you are feeling overwhelmed, this is a great way to calm that, but if you need anything, just press the button.” She gestured again toward the button on the railing with an image of a person. “But for now, just try to get some rest.”
But I just woke up?
She started turning away from me as she continued typing.

“I’ll bring you back some books for entertainment.” By now her voice was trailing off as she walked toward the door. She dropped the tablet from her attention and turned entirely toward me with a serious look. “Promise me you won’t try to walk again while I’m gone, please.” Her eyebrows were raised as she waited for a response from me.
I nodded. “Promise.” I added a hand to my heart for effect.

After watching her leave, I looked back toward the massive window letting all the golden hour light in. Outside I could see the tops of some trees and mid-canopy of others swaying in a light wind. The leaves had that golden hue of evening sunlight. They were casting rustling shadows through the window that speckled the floor of the room. I must be a few stories up. I stared at the swaying tree for a moment, caught in the rhythm, before I noticed a low humming noise that felt like it was vibrating my whole body. I lifted my hands to feel my skin. I couldn’t tell if I was mistaken or not, but it felt like my skin was vibrating. The room seemed to swell now: pulling toward me then pushing back out with each breath. The plants were mirroring me, waving, kind and calm. There was a sour unease in my gut, chest and throat. It felt like I was starting to trip on some sort of hallucinogen.

I looked down at my hands. They were swelling and shrinking in my vision. My attention jumped to the buttons on the railing and I swung my rubbery feeling arm over to force my hand down on the button to call the attendant back.

My vision started to blur as my heavy head started to sink, but I forced them open as I lifted my head upright again with a deep inhalation. For a moment the room returned to its previous undistorted state. My eyes wanted so badly to shut, but I willed them otherwise. They darted around the room to stay active in an attempt to force wakefulness.

In the moments when consciousness was full and focused, I would attempt to anchor myself there, only to find myself jolting back awake after an undetermined amount of time unconscious. It was of no use.
